cards.title: Western Europe (500-1500 C.E.)
body: Middle Age (Medieval)- is the period extending from 500-1500 C.E in European history and is marked by the migration of Germanic tribes into Europe to fill the power vacuum created by the fall of the Western Roman Empire. The middle ages is characterized by;
1. A new socio-economic and political system known as Feudalism
2. Retarded economic, cultural and intellectual development
3. Emergence of strong states led by Monarchs
The middle ages is subdivided into 3 periods; Early middle ages, High middle ages and Late middle ages.

cards.title: Completing this point: what characterized the Middle Ages
body: **The three features, explained.** (1) **Feudalism** – a system in which kings granted land (fiefs) to lords in return for military service, and serfs worked the land in return for protection. (2) **Slow economic, cultural and intellectual development** in the early centuries, after the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476: trade and towns declined and learning survived mainly in monasteries. (3) **The rise of strong monarchies** in the later centuries, as kings slowly took power back from the lords.
**The three sub-periods.** Early Middle Ages (476–1000), High Middle Ages (1000–1300) and Late Middle Ages (1300–1450).
**Memory trick:** "F-S-M: Feudalism, Slow growth, Monarchs."
**Exam tip:** "Medieval" comes from Latin *medium aevum*, "the middle age" – the period between ancient Rome and the Renaissance.

cards.title: 1) Early Middle Ages (476-1000)
body: 5th-8th C, various Germanic tribes invaded Europe and created new governments in France, Spain, Italy, England, North Africa and Western Mediterranean.

But by the 6th C, most of their kingdoms were destroyed; the Byzantine Empire destroyed the kingdoms in Italy and North Africa, while the Arabs destroyed the one in Spain. Only the Frankish Kingdom remained.

cards.title: The Frankish Kingdom
body: Was established under the Clovis dynasty and they adopted Roman culture. Their kings and queens had close ties with the Catholic Church. They provided land and received the church’s support in return.
Monasteries were established in the kingdom and were run by monks and nuns. A monk is an individual who leads a life secluded from the world in total devotion to God.

8th C, the Franks were able to defeat the moors (North African Muslims) under the leadership of Charles the Great (Charlemagne) who revived learning and arts. He was crowned ‘Emperor’ in 800 C.E by the Pope. After his death, the kingdom was divided into; A) Western Frankish Kingdom (France)
B) Eastern Frankish Kingdom (Germany)
C) Middle Frankish Kingdom (Italy and Netherlands)
Decline-1) Internal crisis
2) Moor invasion
3) Magyar (people from western Asia) invasion
4) Viking (Germanic tribes of Scandinavia) invasion

cards.title: Feudalism
body: After the decline of Charlemagne’s Empire, people began to seek protection from local landowner aristocrats (nobles and lords), thus an unwritten feudal contract was agreed on between the people and the lords.

Vassalage was the central idea of feudalism where the Vassals served the lords in a military capacity and were in return granted a piece of land that supported their families. This land is known as Fief.

Peasants worked in manors owned by the lords or the fiefs given to the vassals. Manors were agricultural Estates run by lords and worked by peasants known as Serfs. The once free peasants gave up their freedom in return of the protection provided by the lords.

The Serfs were obliged to pay rent to the lords by sharing everything they produced to the lord and pay tithe (a tenth of their products) to the church. Feudalism spread from the Frankish kingdom to England, Germany, Central Europe and Italy by the 11th C.

cards.title: Economy during the Early Middle Ages
body: Their economy was mostly based on agriculture and small local trade which was insufficient because their tools were too primitive. European infrastructure and economy collapsed along with learning and arts.
Europe began to recover after the 10th C as the fall of Charlemagne’s Empire gave rise to new powerful feudal lords in France and Germany, while England was unified under one king.

cards.title: 2) High Middle Ages (1000-1300 C.E)
body: Western Europe emerged from its backwardness as urbanization, military expansion and intellectualism were revived. The progress in the era was caused by;
1. The end of the Moor, Magyar and Viking invasions enabled revival of economy
2. Agricultural Revolution introduced new advances in agricultural technology securing food abundance and the growth of population in the cities.

cards.title: Completing this point: why Western Europe revived in the High Middle Ages
body: **Cause 1 – security.** The Moor, Magyar and Viking invasions ended, so farming and trade could recover.
**Cause 2 – the agricultural revolution.** New tools and methods (the heavy iron plough, the horse collar, water mills and the **three-field system**) produced more food, and the population grew.
**Cause 3 – trade and towns.** Surplus food and peace revived trade fairs and towns; merchants and craftsmen formed **guilds**.
**Cause 4 – learning.** The first **universities** (Bologna, Paris, Oxford) appeared, and the Crusades brought contact with Byzantine and Muslim learning.
**Memory trick:** "Safe – Fed – Trading – Learning."

cards.title: Towns and Cities
body: New cities and towns grew in the Netherlands, Germany, France and Italy, while cities like Rome, Marseille, Paris and Trier grew around the old cities. Most of the Medieval cities had 3 centers; a marketplace, a church or cathedral and a castle.
The manufacture of cloth, metal, shoes and leather products grew in the towns and cities. During the 12th C, artisans organized themselves into business associations known as Guilds.
The Guilds set standards quality for the products produced, specified the methods of production and fixed the prices for the finished goods.

cards.title: Schools and Universities
body: Before the 12th C, Education was only provided by churches and monasteries to young boys until the development city schools which later developed into Universities in the cities of France and Italy. The first European university was in Bologna, while the University of Paris was the first one in Western Europe.

cards.title: Vernacular Literature and Architecture
body: Latin was the most widespread language in Europe during the medieval period; it was used in schools and churches. But in the 12th C, new literature was written in the vernacular languages like Spanish, French, Italian, English and German.
Architecture also grew in the 12th C as many cathedrals in Gothic style were built,
Growth of European Kingdoms- The revival of commerce, growth of cities and economy increased the power of the lords and kings in Europe and gave rise to new monarchies in Europe.

cards.title: Completing this point: Gothic cathedrals
body: **When.** The Gothic style appeared in the **12th century** and was perfected in the 13th. The 11th and 12th centuries saw an explosion of cathedral building.

**What makes a building Gothic.** Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and **flying buttresses** carried the weight outward, so walls could be thinner and higher, with tall spires and huge **stained-glass windows** that filled the church with coloured light.

**Why it matters.** The Gothic cathedral is one of the greatest artistic achievements of the High Middle Ages and shows the wealth of the towns and the power of the Church. Famous examples: Notre-Dame in Paris and Chartres cathedral.
**Memory trick:** "Pointed, Ribbed, Buttressed, Glass" (P-R-B-G).

cards.title: England
body: England was invaded by the Germanic tribes of Angles and Saxons and fell under Anglo-Saxon kings after it was united by King Alfred the Great in the 9th C.

13th C, nobles rebelled against King John because they hated the increasing power of the kings and John was forced to sign the document of rights known as the Magna Carta (the Great Charter) in 1215. This limited the power of the kings and gave rise to the Parliament in the 13th C. The Parliament had the right to levy taxes and pass laws; it was composed of two houses; the House of the Lords and the House of Commons.

cards.title: The French Kingdom
body: Emerged from the Western Frankish Kingdom under the Capetian dynasty of Hugh Capet in 987 C.E.
During the reign of King Philip II (1180-1223), the French monarchy grew and French lands under the English rule were recovered. France became the largest monarchial state in Europe in 1300.

In 1302, King Philip IV set up a Parliament known as Estates General consisting 3 Estates; the first Estate was composed of the clergy, the second was of the nobles and the third of townspeople and peasants.

cards.title: The Catholic Church
body: Since the 5th C, the popes have had both spiritual and political powers and controlled all the affairs of the church and set up territories in central Italy known as the Papal States. Bishops were appointed by the kings of the Eastern Frankish (Holy Roman Empire) and were obliged to carry out feudal and military services.

Conflict arose when the Church wanted to appoint its own officials; it was solved by the Concordat of Worms (1122). The agreement stated that the church officials were to be appointed by both the church and the kings.

cards.title: 3) Late Middle Ages (1300-1450 C.E )
body: The period is characterized by;
A) Plague- the Black Death
B) Economic decline
C) Decline of the Catholic Church
D) Political instability

cards.title: Completing this point: the crisis of the Late Middle Ages
body: **A) The Black Death (1347–1351).** A plague carried by fleas on rats killed perhaps one-third of Europe's population.
**B) Economic decline.** Fewer workers and farmers meant less production; trade fell, and peasants who survived demanded higher wages, leading to revolts.
**C) Decline of the Catholic Church.** The popes moved to Avignon and then the **Great Schism** (two and later three rival popes) damaged the Church's prestige.
**D) Political instability.** Long wars, especially the **Hundred Years' War** between England and France (1337–1453), weakened kings and nobles.
**Memory trick:** "Plague, Poverty, Popes, Politics" (the four P's).

cards.title: A) The Black Death
body: The Black Death (Bubonic plague) was the worst natural disaster in European history spread by infested black rats brought into Sicily from the Black Sea by Italian merchants in the 1347. It quickly spread into Italy, France (1348), Germany, the Low countries (modern Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands), England (1349), Scandinavia, Russia and Eastern Europe (1351).

Out of the total European population of 70 million, 38 million died in 1347-1351. In England, Germany and Italy, entire villages disappeared. The plague brought the outbreak of anti-Semitism as people accused the Jews of poisoning the wells.

cards.title: B) The Hundred Years War (1337-1453)
body: A series of wars between France and England caused by territorial dispute. The war affected both their economies and societies. England faced human and economic losses; it also faced the War of Roses, a civil war caused as the nobles fought to control the monarchy until the coming of the Tudor dynasty in 1485.
In the 15th C, new European monarchies were established in France, England and Spain after recovering from the 14th C economic decline and civil wars.

cards.title: Model answer: characteristics of the Middle Ages
cards.problem: (Exam question) What were the main characteristics of the Middle Ages in Western Europe (500–1500 C.E.)?

steps.text: Define the period: 500–1500 C.E., starting when Germanic tribes moved in to fill the power vacuum left by the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
Characteristic 1: a new socio-economic and political system – feudalism, built on vassals serving lords in return for land.
Characteristic 2: slow (retarded) economic, cultural and intellectual development.
Characteristic 3: the emergence of strong states led by monarchs; the period is divided into Early, High and Late Middle Ages.

cards.answer: Feudalism, slow economic and intellectual development, and the rise of strong monarchies – in a period that followed the fall of Rome and the Germanic migrations.

cards.title: The Byzantine Empire and the Crusades (500-1500 C.E)
body: The Eastern Roman Empire with its center at Constantinople (modern Istanbul) existed after the fall of the Roman Empire. King Justinian restored the Roman Empire in the Mediterranean including Italy, parts of Spain, North Africa, Asia Minor, Palestine and Syria in 552.
Architecture grew under Justinian, the most famous structure was Hagia Sophia (the church of Holy Wisdom 532-537). After his death, the Empire was lost to the Lombards of Italy.

cards.title: From Eastern Roman Empire to Byzantine Empire
body: The Eastern Roman Empire was challenged by the Islamic forces who occupied Syria and Palestine in the 7th C and the Bulgarians who had created a strong Empire in 679 limiting the empire into eastern Balkans and Asia Minor, this empire was called the Byzantine Empire.

It was a Greek-Christian state with Greek as their official language and Orthodox Christianity as the official religion. They believed the emperor was chosen by God and had absolute power. The Patriarch (head of the Eastern Orthodox Church) was chosen by the emperor.

Economy- Agriculture was the main source of wealth; they produced grain, olive oil, wine and cheese. Trade was conducted between Asia and Europe, they imported Silk (China), Spices (Southeast Asia and India), ivory (India), wheat and fur (Russia) and Flax and honey (Balkans). They exported cotton, glassware, timber and silk.
Height-The Empire expanded under the Macedonians from 867 to 1081, economy and power was restored.
Decline 1. Weak Rulers
2. Civil war between military rulers and the aristocrats in the 11th C
3. Schism- the split of Christianity into the Catholic and the Orthodox Churches
4. Seljuk (Turkish) invasion Seljuks in 1071. Emperor Alexis I had to ask for European help.

cards.title: The Crusades
body: The Crusades were a series of religious wars fought between Muslims and Christians caused by the Seljuk invasion of the Byzantine Empire and Alexis’s plea for Christian help from Europe. European Knights joined the war because they were motivated by; religious feelings, adventure, to gain wealth and title, and create trade opportunities.

1) The first Crusade (1096-1099)-3 French warrior groups went to Constantinople and set up 4 states in Antioch (1098), Edessa, Tripoli and Jerusalem (1099), this resulted in the growth of the port cities of Geona, Pisa and Venice.
2) The Second Crusade (1147-1149)- the Muslims recaptured Edessa in the 1140s, but the crusade failed.

3) The Third Crusade (1189-1192)- begun after the Muslims controlled Jerusalem led by commander Saladin in 1187. European forces under Emperor Frederick Barbarossa (Germany), Richard I the Lionhearted (England), and Philip II Augustus (France). Frederick’s forces drowned in a river, Philip went back home and Richard reached an agreement with Saladin allowing Christian pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

4) The Fourth Crusade- was initiated by Pope Innocent III and the crusade focused on sacking Constantinople in 1204. The Byzantines recovered the city in 1261 and reestablished the Empire in a reduced size.
The Fifth and Sixth Crusades aimed to control the Holy Lands but they both failed.

cards.title: Positive Effects of the Crusades
body: 1) Italian cities and ports grew from transporting supplies to the Byzantine Empire by replacing Muslim merchants
2) It helped break down Feudalism, serfs were freed as the lords and kings were busy fighting.
3) Nation-States of Portugal, Spain, England and France grew due to the wealth obtained from trade.
4) Learning was revived as the Greco-Roman books of the Muslims were taken to Europe by the Crusaders

cards.title: Negative Effects of the Crusades
body: 1) Human and material losses on both sides
2 Anti-Zionism sentiments grew in Europe

cards.title: The Arabs and thE Rise of Islam
body: Arabs- are Semitic speaking people of the Arabian Peninsula who led a nomadic life by moving around the desert for food and water organized into tribes ruled by sheiks. The sheiks were chosen by the Mejlis (council of elders).
The early Arabs were involved in farming, herding and caravan trade (land trade). They were polytheistic and traced their ancestry to Abraham and his son Ishmael.

The political disorders in Mesopotamia, Byzantine and Persia resulted in the shift of trade from the old route to a new route that passed by Yemen and the Indian Ocean, thus increased the importance of the Arabian Peninsula. Cities like Mecca benefited from the new trade routes creating a gap between the rich and poor.

cards.title: The Life of Mohammad
body: Mohammad was born in Mecca in 570 C.E and worked in trade after marrying Khadija. He was worried about the growing gap between the rich and the poor thus used to meditate. He received revelations from God through an angel that were later written in the Quran.

His teachings of Islam (submission to the will of Allah) in Mecca were rejected by the Qurayesh (wealthy tribe) who begun persecuting his followers. Some of his followers came to the Red Sea to gain refuge from the Aksumite king.

In 622, Mohammed fled into Medina (city of the prophet) in what is known as the Hijrah and formed the first Islamic community known as the Umma in Medina where he was both the political and religious leader. He returned to Mecca in 630 and preached Islam until his death after 2 years.

cards.title: The Teachings of Mohammad
body: Islam is a monotheistic religion like Christianity and Judaism and believes Mohammad to be the last prophet. It stresses on obeying Allah through the 5 pillars of Islam;
1. Shahadah- belief in one God, Allah and his messenger Mohammad
2. Salaat- to pray 5 times a day
3. Zakat- giving a percentage of one’s wealth to the poor
4. Sawm- fasting during Ramadan (holy month)
5. Hajj- pilgrimage to Mecca at least once in a lifetime to the Kaaba
The Shariah is the Muslim law-code created by the Muslim scholars known as the Ulama after Mohammad’s death.

cards.title: Completing this point: the Five Pillars and the Shariah
body: **The Five Pillars are the five basic duties of every Muslim.** 1) **Shahadah** – declaring faith in one God, Allah, and Mohammad as his messenger; 2) **Salat** – praying five times a day facing Mecca; 3) **Zakat** – giving a share of one's wealth to the poor; 4) **Sawm** – fasting from dawn to sunset in **Ramadan**; 5) **Hajj** – the pilgrimage to the Kaaba in Mecca at least once in a lifetime, if able.

**The Shariah.** After Mohammad's death, scholars (the **Ulama**) developed the Shariah, the Islamic law code, from the Quran and the sayings and practice of the Prophet (the Hadith and Sunna). It guides daily life, family matters and trade.
**Memory trick – "Say, Pray, Pay, Fast, Go":** Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj.

cards.title: The Appearance of Islamic Empires
body: In 632, one of Mohammad’s closest followers, Abu Baker, became a Caliph (the successor of Mohammad). The Islamic movement grew towards the Byzantine Empire by defeating them at Yamruk in 636, Syria (640), Egypt and North Africa (642) and the Persian Empire in 650. Islamic expansion was successful because;
1. Both the Byzantine and Persia were weakened due to constant wars
2. The locals were dissatisfied with Imperial rule and accepted the new Arab regime
3. The Muslim fighters were motivated because believed that fighting and dying would fulfilling their religious duties
4. Each newly conquered land was secured by moving large Arab populations to it
In 750 C.E, the center of Islamic rule shifted from Medina to Damascus with the rise of the Umayyad dynasty.

cards.title: Completing this point: why Islam expanded so fast
body: **Reason 1 – weak neighbours.** The Byzantine and Persian empires had exhausted each other in long wars.

**Reason 2 – welcome from local people.** Many subjects resented high imperial taxes and religious persecution and accepted the new Arab rulers, who often allowed Christians and Jews to keep their faith in return for a tax.
**Reason 3 – religious motivation.** Muslim fighters believed that fighting for the faith was a religious duty.
**Reason 4 – settlement.** Arab populations were moved into conquered lands to secure them.
**Key dates.** Yarmuk 636, Syria 640, Egypt 642, Persia about 650. The Umayyads moved the capital from Medina to **Damascus** (661); the Abbasids later built **Baghdad** (750 onwards).
**Memory trick:** "Weak – Welcome – Willing – Settled."

cards.title: 1) The Umayyad Dynasty (661-750)
body: Abu Baker was succeeded by Caliph Omer, who was in return succeeded by Caliph Osman. Many Muslims weren’t satisfied with Osman because they wanted Ali (Mohammad’s cousin) to be the Caliph, Osman was assassinated in 656 and was succeeded by Ali. Caliph Ali was also assassinated by the Mu’awiyahs (Syria’s governors).

In 661, Amir Mu’awiyah became the Caliph and established the Umayyad Dynasty with Damascus as his capital, they converted the Berbers (North African natives) into Islam and conquered Spain (710) with its center at Cordoba, Mesopotamia and central Asia. They failed in Byzantine and France (717 &732) after losing the Battle of Tours (Gaul, France).
Decline- 1. Internal crisis as the non-Arab Muslims (Byzantines &Persians) were being ignored by the rulers.
2. Ali’s second son, Hussein, led a revolt against the Umayyads resulting in the split of Muslims into Shiite and Sunni.

The Shiites (a minority found in Iran and Iraq) accepted only the descendants of Ali as the Caliphs while the Sunnis (a majority found all over the world) believed that any Muslim including the Umayyads could be Caliphs.

cards.title: 2) The Abbasid Dynasty (750-1258)
body: 750, Abu al-Abbas, a descendant of Mohammad, set up the Abbasid by overthrowing the Umayyads with its capital at Baghdad (Iraq). They benefited from river and caravan trade in the Persian Gulf and the Mediterranean region.

The society was composed of Arabs and non-Arabs who had equal civil and military rights. The dynasty reached its height under Harun al-Rashid who supported artists, writers and learning. The dynasty conquered provinces of the Roman Empire and trade routes to the East.
Decline- 1. Wars of succession
2. Financial Corruption
3. Shortage of qualified Arabs in key positions Arabs led to non-Arab domination as they began to rule provinces and broke away from the central government.

cards.title: 3) The Seljuk Turks
body: Were nomadic Turkish soliders from central Asia who converted into Islam after being hired by the Fatimids of Egypt under the Abbasid dynasty.

The Seljuks grew stronger after the fall of the Abbasids and expanded into Iran, Armenia, Baghdad (1055) and Byzantine (1071). Their invasion of the Byzantine Empire made the Emperor (Alexis I) ask for European help leading to the Crusades

cards.title: 4) The Mongols
body: Were non-Muslim Pastoral people from the Gobi desert who controlled mush of Asia including Persia and Mesopotamia by defeating the Baghdad Caliphate (1258) under their leader Genghis Khan. The Mongols were violent, they burned cities and destroyed villages.
Their attempts to control Egypt failed because of strong resistance from the Mamluks (Turkish slave-soldiers ruling Egypt). The Mongols eventually began to intermarry with locals and grew in numbers.

cards.title: Completing this point: common features of Islamic civilizations
body: **1. Extensive trade.** Arab merchants traded by ship and camel caravan with China (silk, porcelain), India and Southeast Asia (spices, sandalwood), Africa (gold, ivory, slaves) and the Byzantine Empire. Banking and coins made exchange easier.
**2. Great cities.** Baghdad (the "City of Peace") under the Abbasids, Cairo under the Fatimids, and Damascus. Each city had palaces, a great mosque, public baths and a covered market (**bazaar**).

**3. A class society.** In theory all are equal before Allah, but in practice there was an upper class (rulers, officials, rich merchants) and a lower class. Slavery existed, but freeing slaves was considered a good act.
**4. Rights for women.** Women could own and inherit property and had some right to divorce, although men were dominant.

**5. Rich culture and learning.** Muslim scholars preserved and translated Greek works and made advances in mathematics (algebra, Arabic numerals), astronomy, medicine and philosophy. Architecture featured mosques with domes and minarets and geometric decoration.
**Memory trick:** "T-C-S-W-L: Trade, Cities, Society, Women, Learning."

cards.title: 1) Trade and Cities
body: Caravan and sea trade were conducted with the whole world. Trade was highly simplified by the development of banking and coinage systems and it gave rise to rich cities such as Baghdad, Cairo under the Fatimids and Damascus.
Each city had public buildings with fountains, public baths, bazzars (marketplaces) and great Mosques while in the country sides, people lived off farming and herding.

cards.title: 2) Society
body: Even though Islam considered all people as equals and prohibits Slavery, the Islamic society was divided into upper class (rulers, senior officials and wealthy merchants) and lower class (the rest of the society). Non-Muslim slaves were bought from Africa and Asia to serve in the army and domestic works. The slaves were allowed to buy their own freedom.
In the Quran, Women had the right to own and inherit property but were subjected to male guardians who dictated their marriages while men could have 4 wives. Adultery was forbidden to all.

cards.title: 3) Culture
body: Muslim Arabs absorbed the Greco-Roman culture; they translated the books of Plato and Aristotle into Arabic and kept them in the House of Wisdom (Library in Baghdad). They brought Mathematics from India and Paper from China.

cards.title: 4) Philosophy, Science and History
body: Philosophy developed under Muslim philosophers such as Ibn-Rashid, while mathematics and numerical system were adapted from India. Al Khwarizmi was a famous mathematician who shaped Algebra in the 9th C.

An Observatory was set up in Baghdad and it was used in Astronomy. Ibn Sina was the scientist who wrote the medical Encyclopedia. Ibn-Khaldun was a famous historian, he wrote Introduction to History in the 14th C.

cards.title: 5) Islamic Literature, Art and Architecture
body: The greatest literary works include the Quran, the Rubaiyat written by Omer Khayyam and The Thousand and One nights (Arabian nights). Islamic art is a combination of Arab, Turkish and Persian traditions; they built great palaces and mosques such as the Great Mosque of Samarra (Iran), the mosque of Cordoba (southern Spain) and large brick castles in Syria.
Islamic art doesn’t contain any imitations of God or living beings thus, geometric figures were used.

cards.title: Early Civilzations in Mesoamerica
body: The Americas stretch from the Arctic Ocean in the north to Cape Horn at the tip of South America, it consists North America, Meso-America and South America. Its inhabitants came from Asia to North America through the Bering Strait during the Ice Age (100,000-8,000 B.C.E) and expanded into the Americas in around 10,000 B.C.E.
The 2 major civilizations of Mesoamerica were the Mayan and Aztec.

cards.title: 1) Mayan Civilization (300-900 C.E)
body: Politics- Flourished on the Yucatan Peninsula and included much of Central and Southern America, it was composed of city-states governed by divine hereditary ruling class. They used Pyramids as tombs of the upper class.

Society- the included the upper class ( Nobles, scribes and preists), middle class (artisans, officials and merchants) and peasants. There was a division of labor; men hunted while women did the domestic work.
Economy- agriculture was the main activity followed by trade through barter. Their cities had public buildings, temples, palaces and pyramids.
Religion- they were polytheistic, their gods were associated with serpents, the Sun, moon and fire. They practiced Human sacrifice in ceremonies and to please the gods.
Writing System- used a sophisticated system based on hieroglyphs (pictures) written on bark, clay, bone and stone, to record the lives of rulers, religious and astronomical information.

Calendar- their 2 types of calendar were based on the belief in the cycles of life; creation and destruction. They believed the world was created in 3113 B.C and was going to vanish in December 23 of 2012. The Solar calendar, closest to the Julian Calendar, had 365 days divided into 18 months of 20 days and extra 5 days. The Sacred Calendar had 260 days divided into 13 weeks of 2o days and was used for religious purposes.
Decline (790-889 C.E)- 1) Natural Disasters
2) Peasant revolts
3) Internal warfare
4) Foreign invasions

cards.title: 2) Aztec Civilization
body: The Aztecs moved from Western Mexico and set up their capital at Tenochtitlan (Lake Texcoco, modern Mexico City) after being pushed by other people in 1325. They began to build their cities and expanded over Mexico.

Politics-the empire was a collection of semi-independent territories under local lords. The King was believed to have a divine rule and was assisted by a council of lords who were given land for their services.

Society- was composed of the upper class, commoners, indentured workers (contracted workers in a lord’s estate) and slaves. Boys were raised to be warriors while girls in domestic works or to become priestesses.

Religion- they were polytheistic, their chief god was Huitzilopochtli (god of sun and war). They believed in the struggle between good and evil which had led to the creation and destruction of 4 suns and the fifth is destined to end by an earthquake. To delay this destruction, they practiced Human sacrifice. They used pyramids as shrines.
Economy- Irrigation farming was their main source of income, they built terraces, fertilizers and the Chinampas (floating gardens) they also had trade and manufacture.
Writing System and Calendar- they used a crude form of writing. The Aztecs had 2 types of calendars; with 260 and 365 days.
Decline- 1. Internal crisis

2. Spanish invasion- led by Hernan Cortes allied with Aztec city- states and was welcomed by King Montezuma as gods in 1519. The people started to rebel in 1520 and were killed by the Spaniards and by an epidemic (Small Pox).

cards.title: Inca Civilization
body: Grew from a small community in Cuzco (southern Peru) into an Empire under the leadership of Pachacuti in 1440’s.

Politics- Pachacuti’s successors expanded the Empire through war into Ecuador, central Chile and the edge of the Amazon basin; it had a population of 12 million people. It had the largest army of 200,000 troops and all Incans were obliged to render unpaid labor service in building projects such as the 40,000 kms long roads. The Empire was divided into 4 quarters ruled by governors, and each quarter into provinces.
Economy- depended on irrigated agriculture, they produced 20 types of corn and 240 types of potatoes. The land was very rich in gold and silver and this attracted the Spaniards.

Culture and Science- they had extensive knowledge in architecture, medicine, calendar, theatre, poetry and plays. They had no writing system but used the Quipu (knotted strings), but most of their art and architecture was destroyed by the Spaniards and most of the gold was taken to Spain.

lessons.title: The Rise of Civilizations in sub-Saharan Africa

cards.title: The Rise of Civilizations in sub-Saharan Africa
body: Africa is the birthplace of Humanity and civilizations in Egypt and Nubia in the north, Axum, Ghana and Mali in the west, Swahili city-states in the east and the Great Zimbabwe in the South.

Farming and animal husbandry were introduced into Africa through North Africa from Western Asia at around 5000 B.C. The Bantus of West Africa prospered from food production and population growth until shortage of land caused their migrations into Central, Eastern and Southern Africa in 200 C.E.

Iron work was introduced in East Africa by the Assyrians who conquered Egypt. It spread from Meroe (Nubia) south while West Africa learned about it from Carthage. Iron was used to make tools and weapons.
Agricultural revolution began under the Bantus resulting in the rise of social organization, Villages and civilization between 500-1500 C.E.

cards.title: Step by step: how farming, iron and the Bantu laid the foundations
body: **Step 1 – hunting and gathering.** The earliest Africans lived by hunting and gathering.

**Step 2 – farming (about 5000 BCE).** Crop farming and herding reached the North African coast, probably from Western Asia. East Africans grew local millet and sorghum; West Africans grew yams and oil palms; farming reached Southern Africa later.
**Step 3 – iron.** Iron working reached Meroe by 500 BCE and spread south; West Africa learned it from Carthage. Iron hoes, axes and spearheads made farming and defence easier.

**Step 4 – the Bantu migrations.** By 200 CE more food meant more Bantu people in West Africa; shortage of land and water pushed them into Central, East and Southern Africa over two thousand years, spreading farming, iron and village life.
**Result.** These foundations allowed civilizations to rise between 500 and 1500 CE.
**Memory trick:** "Food → Iron → Migration → States."

cards.title: East Africa
body: East African societies were the results of interactions between the indigenous communities and the Bantu immigrants, the major states are;

cards.title: Completing this point: the major states of East Africa
body: **A. The coastal city-states.** From the 8th century Muslim traders from Arabia and the Persian Gulf settled along the coast, and trading ports grew up: **Mogadishu** (Somalia), **Mombasa and Malindi** (Kenya), **Kilwa** (Tanzania) and Zanzibar. Kilwa was the richest, with the Great Mosque and the Husuni Kubwa palace (14th century). Intermarriage of Africans and Arabs produced the **Swahili** culture and language – Bantu with many Arabic words, "people of the coast".

**B. The states of the Lakes region.** The Bantu **Chwezi** settled western Uganda 600–700 years ago. Between the 14th and 16th centuries Nilotic herders from Sudan formed the kingdoms of **Bunyoro**, **Ankole** and **Buganda**. Bunyoro became dominant by the 16th century as a loose confederation of chiefdoms that paid tribute to the king.
**Why they rose.** Fertile land for farming and well-developed internal and external trade.
**Memory trick:** "Coast = Kilwa and Swahili; Lakes = Bunyoro and Buganda."

cards.title: A) East African Coastal States
body: The Bantus already practiced trade in the East African coasts, but in the 7th C trade grew as Muslims from the Arabian Peninsula and the Persian Gulf settled at ports along the Indian Ocean and created the wealthy trade ports of Mogadishu (Somalia), Mombasa (Kenya) and Kilwa (Tanzania). Muslim merchants grew very wealthy.

Swahili- is a mixture of African and Arabian cultures created due to the intermarriages between the Arabs and Africans. Swahili is a Sahel term meaning ‘the people of the coasts’. As a language, Swahili is now spoken as a lingua franca (day to day language, a mixture) in East Africa.
Those states declined during the 16th C with the coming of Portuguese and Omani-Arab invaders.

cards.title: B) States of the Lake Region
body: The Chwezi (Bantu sub-group) established settlements in Western Uganda until they were displaced by Nilotic speaking herders from Sudan. The Nilotic groups formed the Kingdoms of Bunyoro (south of Lake Albert), Ankole (west of Lake Victoria) and Buganda (modern Uganda and northern Tanzania).
The reasons for the rise of the lake-region kingdoms were; fertile land and trade (internal and external).

Bunyoro- dominated the region through a loose confederation of chiefdoms (political organizations led by chiefs) in the 16th C. their economy was a mixture of farming, hunting and herding. Each chiefdom paid tribute and provided an army to the king. They continuously raided the cattle of their neighbors such as the Buganda.

Buganda- emerged as a centralized kingdom between Bunyoro and Ankole, 500 years ago. Its fertile soil and regular rainfall caused the growth of intensive banana cultivation, increasing its population. The Kabaka (king) ruled through regional chiefs by giving them land, they has extensive road system.

cards.title: West Africa
body: The growth of trans-Saharan trade helped by the introduction of Camels in 750 C.E, led to West African civilizations.

cards.title: A) The Kingdom of Ghana
body: Politics- Established in 500 C.E, it was the first trading state in western Africa located in the upper Niger valley, grassland between the Sahara and the West African tropical forests. Modern Ghana is found south of the forest region. Kumbi Saleh was the capital and the king had the highest authority and trained regular army of 200,000 men.

Economy- depended on agriculture, iron and gold mining, and extensive trade with Muslim merchants who brought metal, textile, horses and salt from North Africa to Ghana in exchange for gold in a system known as Silent trade.

Silent Trade was conducted without a sound, the Arabs placed their goods on the ground and leave, and then the Ghanans come and put their gold beside the other goods and leave. The Arabs return and take the gold if they are satisfies by the price, if not, they would depart until the Ghanans add to their price. Trade across the desert was carried out by the Berbers using Camel caravans known as ‘fleets of the desert’ after 200 C.E.

Decline-The state of Ghana collapsed during the 12th C as trade became dominated by Muslim merchants and Berbers, who carried them across the desert to Ghana, the rise of new trading societies such as Mali, 12th -13th C and various wars.

cards.title: B) The Kingdom of Mali
body: Politics- Was founded by Sundiata Kieta after he defeated Ghana in 1240 and united the people of Mali under a strong government, Timbuktu grew as a very powerful city.

Economy- majority were farmers while trade grew because Mali was rich in gold and their villages were run by local rulers who paid tribute to the king, one of the most powerful kings was Mansa Musa (1312-1337).

Mansa created a strong government and ruled by dividing the kingdom into provinces ruled by governors. He made pilgrimage to Mecca as he was a devout Muslim; he built mosques and studied the Quran. Mali collapsed after the death of Mansa Musa as it was divided because of a civil war; it was dominated by the Songhai kingdom.

cards.title: C) The Kingdom of Songhai
body: Was established under the rule of Kossi, who converted into Islam and set up the Dia dynasty in 1009 C.E. It benefited from the Muslim trade route linking Arabia, North and West Africa. The Sunni dynasty was created by Sunni Ali in 1464, the conquest of Mali and its cities (Timbuktu and Jenne) expanded salt and gold trade.
Mohammed Ture brought the Empire to its height by creating the Askia (usurper) dynasty in 1493. He expanded the Empire and ruled by dividing it into provinces, brought peace and economic prosperity.
The Empire collapsed in around 1600 as the forces of the Moroccan Sultan occupied its lands.

steps.text: Muslim merchants brought metal, textiles, horses and salt from North Africa to exchange for Ghana's gold.

cards.answer: A wordless exchange of North African goods for gold; controlling this trans-Saharan gold trade made Ghana rich and powerful.

cards.title: A) The Luba Kingdom
body: The Luba were iron-making farmers who lived in the Lake Kisale region, found southeast of the modern Democratic Republic of Congo, from the 4th C.E onwards.
Economy- they developed sophisticated agriculture, fishing, hunting, trade and crafts.

Government- 1300, they organized themselves into chiefdoms which later became a centralized kingdom under the Nkongolo dynasty. The dynasty was replaced by a new one under which, the kingdom prospered. The king ruled by dividing the kingdom into small villages ruled by a headman or a provincial governor.

Decline- The kingdom had a very small army; it also experienced rivalry for power with in the court. In 1450 C.E, one group from the royal family left and set up its own kingdom among the Lunda people (found southwest of the Luba kingdom).

cards.title: B) The Lunda Kingdom
body: The Lunda were disorganized and lived in small farming villages until the coming of the Luba royal family in 1450. The Luba intermarried with the Luanda creating the new Lunda Empire in the 16th C.
The empire reached its height during the 17th -16th C due to; the adoption of new American crops such as maize and cassava, and long distance trade.

cards.title: C) The Kingdom of Kongo
body: Emerged from the small Bantu states created in modern Angola and lower Congo River in 1400. The kingdom was a federation of small states with its capital at Mbanza Kongo. It stretched from the Atlantic in the west to the Kwango River in the east, and had established diplomatic relations with the Portuguese.
It declined in the 18th C.

cards.title: Southern Africa
body: It was after the 11th C that states emerged in the southern region of Africa, before that the people were organized into independent farming and herding clans. Villages were built inside massive walls to protect the people and their cattle and begun to unite to establish the first states.
The State of Zimbabwe emerged with its capital at Great Zimbabwe, a city surrounded by stone walls (the Great Enclosure). It prospered from gold trade with the Swahilis and Asia.
The city was abandoned in the 15th C as the soil lost its fertility, probably caused by overgrazing, natural disasters or crop failures.

cards.title: Great Zimbabwe in numbers
body: **Before states.** Until the 11th century people south of the Zambezi lived in independent villages led by clan heads, with a mixed economy of farming, cattle herding and trade. Villages were walled to protect animals at night.
**The rise.** From the 11th century villages united into the first states. Zimbabwe, with its capital at Great Zimbabwe, was the richest and strongest state in the region from about **1300 to 1450**.
**Wealth.** Gold traded through the Swahili coastal towns, even reaching China.
**The city.** Up to **11,000** people lived there. The **Great Enclosure** was an oval wall **244 m long, 5 m thick and 10 m high**, built of granite blocks stacked **without mortar**.
**The decline.** By the mid-15th century the city was abandoned, probably because overgrazing exhausted the soil, or because of drought and crop failure.
**Memory trick:** "1300–1450, 11,000 people, no mortar."

cards.title: A) The Sui Dynasty (581-618 C.E)
body: After the fall of the Han dynasty in 220 C.E, China faced 300 years of chaos and civil war until the rise of the Sui dynasty in 581. China was once again unified under the emperor’s authority.

Sui Yangdi was its last ruler and he used forced labor to build the Grand Canal (built to link the yellow and Yangtze Rivers), he imposed high taxes, was corrupt and faced military failures resulting in the rebellion where he was killed.

cards.title: B) The Tang Dynasty (618-907)
body: Replaced the Sui in 618, the dynasty introduced many reforms and created a stable economy by giving land to the peasants in order to break the power of the nobles. The rulers brought peace between China and its neighbors while expanding the Empire towards Tibet and Korea.

Inventions- the invention of printing in the 7th C is one of the most remarkable invention as it helped spread literature, art and Chinese poetry. Gunpowder was also invented by the Tang; it was used to make explosives.
Decline- was caused by rivalry for power, corruption and rebellion even though the rulers had hired the Uighurs (Turkish- speaking northern tribes) into their army.

cards.title: C) The Song Dynasty (960-1279)
body: Chinese economy and culture prospered but the dynasty faced confrontations when its northern neighbors occupied large parts of Chinese territories. This forced the rulers to move their government south to Hangzhou.
Government- politics and society was led by Confucian ideas, it was a monarchy divided into provinces, districts and villages.

Economy- depended on agriculture, land was owned only by the aristocrats during the civil war but the Song gave land to the peasants, increased food production by improving farming. Long-distance trade was revived under the Tang and Song dynasties as China began exporting tea, Silk and porcelain. The city of Changan (silk city) emerged as a result of silk trade.
Technology- steel and cotton textile were introduced
Decline- 1200, the Mongols controlled all of China and overthrew the song dynasty creating Mongol rule in China.

cards.title: The Mongol Empire
body: The Mongols were pastoral people from Gobi desert, united under Temujin, later elected as Gengis Khan (strong ruler) in 1206. The empire expanded into Asia and Europe with its capital at Karakorum (a city in modern Mongolia).

After his death in 1227, the Empire was divided among his sons into Khanates (separate territories each ruled by his sons) and expanded by defeating the Abbasids, Persia and the Song dynasty and controlled China using the Gunpowder technology. They also controlled Vietnam but failed in Java, Sumatra and Japan.

China- 1279, Kublai Khan (Gengis’s grandson) established the Yuan dynasty in China with its capital at Khanbaliq (the city of the Khan, modern Beijing). The Mongols were accepted by the Chinese people because of the economic prosperity they brought.
Decline- was caused by too much spending on foreign conquest, corruption, internal instability and the 1368 peasant revolution led by Zhu Yuanzhang overthrew the Mongols and set up the Ming Dynasty.

cards.title: The Rise of the Japanese state
body: The people settled in the Yamato Plain near modern Osaka and Kyoto, organized into farming clans ruled by aristocrats who protected each clan in return for an annual share of their products.

Centralized government was created based on the Chinese model by Prince Shotoku Taishi in the 7th C. Japanese territories were divided into districts ruled by senior officials. Power fell into the hands of the aristocrats after the death of Shotoku in 622 C.E; they controlled lands and demanded taxes.

The decline of the central government gave rise to the Samurai (those who serve), military servants of the aristocrats. The Samurai lived by a strict warrior code known as Bushido (the way of the warrior).

cards.title: The Kamakura Shogunate (1192-1333)
body: Was a centralized government created by a powerful aristocrat known as Minamoto Yoritomo in the 12th C, who set up his power near Tokyo. The government was led by powerful military generals known as Shoguns.

Economy- depended mainly in farming but they had limited farmland thus, they grew rice in flooded fields. They also Manufactured and traded raw materials with Korea and China in exchange of silk, porcelain, books and coins.

Religion- the early societies worshiped spirits Kami (lived in trees, rivers, streams and mountains), their state religion was Shinto (the sacred way). The Emperors were believed to have divine powers and they paid tribute to the different gods. Buddhism was also introduced in the 6th C.

Society- women enjoyed equal rights as men until they became subordinates to men. Japanese literature was developed by women such as the Tale of Genji written by Murasaki Shikibu. Architecture grew during the 14th C.

cards.title: Korea
body: Korean history has been greatly affected by its geographical proximity with China and Japan, as it was invaded by China in 109 B.C.E until the Koreans drove them out of the Korean Peninsula in 300 C.E.
Three new kingdoms emerged in Korea, but the Kingdom of Silla begun to rule until the king was assassinated and Korea fell into chaos.

The Koryo dynasty emerged in the 10th C and used Chinese political system to unify Korea until Mongol invasion in the 13th C. Koreans suffered under the Mongols, they were forced to build ships for Kublai Khan’s invasion of Japan. Mongol rule ended after the collapse of the Mongol Empire in China.
In 1392, the Yi Dynasty was set up under Yi Song-gye. It united Korea and ruled until Chinese invasion in the 17th C.

cards.title: Islamic Expansion
body: 8th- 10th C, Islam spread into India by taking advantage of its political disunity after the Guptas. The expansion was also helped by the rise of the Ghazni state formed by rebellious Turkish slaves in Afghanistan. Mahmud Ghazni extended his rule through most of India before his death in 1030.
Indians tried to resist Ghazni’s invasion but their armies were primitive (used elephants) thus failed. In 1200 the Muslims created the Sultanate of Delhi.
The Sultanate declined due to violent attacks from the Mongols led by Timur Lenk. The Mongols remained in India until the attacks of Moguls and the Portuguese began to endanger India.
Economy- majority were farmers and peasants who paid taxes to local rulers. Even though internal trade collapsed due to civil wars, foreign trade grew and was carried out mostly by Hindu merchants.

cards.title: The Renaissance
body: Renaissance means rebirth, it is a period of European history characterized by the revival of the ancient Greek and Roman culture, in particular relation to art, literature, and architecture.

Renaissance marked the end of the medieval period and the beginning of the modern age. It begun in the middle of the 14th C in Florence, Italy because Italy was the center of the Greek-Roman culture and its location in the Mediterranean Sea enabled contact with both the ancient and the new world.

cards.title: Causes of the Renaissance
body: New Interest in the Old Texts and the Introduction of Printing Press- Much of the Greek-Roman texts had been lost from Western Europe, only a few were in Constantinople after the collapse of the Byzantine Empire in 1453. The invention and development of printing facilitated the production of old and new texts.

The Black Death and New Wealth- Black Death was a devastating epidemic that spread across in the 14th C, killing one third of the European population. This became an advantage because the survivors begun to gain new wealth.
Patronage of Art by the New Ruling Class- members of the new ruling class in Italy begun to legitimize themselves by supporting and sponsoring new artists.

cards.title: Characteristics of Renaissance
body: Renaissance was mostly an urban phenomenon
It was the age of recovery from the disasters of the middle ages such as the plague and political instabilities
The emergence of Individualism
The Emergence of new intellectual and artistic movements, Humanism
The emergence of new political ideas
The development of Vernacular literature
Paintings, Sculptures, and Architecture- Some of the famous renaissance artists include
Leonardo Da Vinci- was an artist and an engineer whose works include, The Mona Lisa (1506), The Last Supper.
Raphael- painted the Virgin Mary, The Mond Crucifixion (1503), Saint George and the Dragon…
Michelangelo- was a painter and sculptor of The Sistine Chapel (1512), The Madonna (1492), The Statue of David (1504), Pieta (1499).
Society- was divided into three estates (nobles, peasants, and townspeople). This division continued into the Renaissance period with some modifications
The Nobility- 14th-15th centuries, old nobles who retained their lands and titles were joined by new nobles making up 3% of the society and began to focus on classical art and education.
Peasants- made up 90% of the society but their freedom was legalized through the Renaissance.

Townspeople- trade, industries, and banking grew during the Renaissance on top of the already existing artisans and guilds collectively known as Burghers. Family bonds became sources of strength and security in the urban society.

cards.title: The Protestant Reformation
body: A Protestant is a person who opposes the Roman Catholic or the Eastern Orthodox Churches. The protestant reformation was a religious reform movement which aimed to correct certain practices and doctrines of the Roman Catholic Church. It resulted in the division of the Catholic Church into protestant sects all over Europe.

cards.title: Causes of the Protestant Reformation
body: Corruption in the Catholic Church- many Church officials had ignored their spiritual duties and were using their positions in the offices to increase their wealth by selling certificates as tickets to heaven.

Active participation of the Popes in worldly manners- the popes became more concerned with Italian politics and ignored their spiritual responsibilities. Example, Pope Julius II was known as warrior-pope because he led armies into wars.
Opposition against the Church’s claim of higher authority by some rulers- some rulers saw the Church loans and taxes as a heavy burden to their economic status.
Intellectual developments of the 15th C and the spread of the new classical learning led to the creation of the Christian Humanism movement, to reform the Catholic Church.

cards.title: Martin Luther and Lutheranism
body: Martin Luther was a German monk and professor who started the reformation in 1517. On October 31, 1517, he wrote 95 Theses about his beliefs that humans can only be saved through their faith and God’s mercy not through their good deeds.
After getting the support of the German princes, he attacked the sale of indulgences granted by the Pope for salvation, the sacraments of the Church and called for the end of celibacy.

Luther’s work was burnt, and he was excommunicated from the Holy Roman Empire in 1521, he was arrested and delivered to Charles V of the Roman Empire but was protected by Elector Frederick of Saxony (Germany). Charles V tried to unite the Roman Empire through Catholicism and the Hapsburg dynasty he failed as he was defeated by the German princes.

In 1555, The Peace of Augsburg accepted the division of Christianity in Germany into Catholicism and Lutheranism. This made Luther’s religious movement a revolution, he set up his own Church and sermons to replace the Catholic practices known as Lutheranism.
The success of Lutheranism in Germany encouraged Scandinavian rulers in Norway, Sweden, and Denmark to challenge the Catholic Church and convert into Lutheranism by the end of the 16th C.

In Switzerland, John Calvin founded Calvinism in France. It included the beliefs of God’s absolute sovereignty and salvation through faith alone. Like Luther, Calvin denied the free will of humans and that only the predestined souls elected by God were saved.
In England, King Henry VIII created the Anglican Church after the Catholic Church forbid him from divorcing his wife to marry another because he only had a daughter, Mary, but wanted a son.
The Catholic Counter Reformation; were measures taken to defend the Church against Protestants
Succession of capable and strong Popes and devoted Clergy.
The Council of Trent (1545) re-introduced traditional Catholic doctrines and reserved the right of interpreting the Bible only to the Church.
Practices such as nepotism (favoritism), simony (selling spirituality i.e., pardons) and sale of indulgences were prohibited.
In 1540, a religious order of the Pope known as the Jesuits (the society of Jesus) was created. They were spiritual soldiers sworn to obey the Pope in their fights against Protestantism.
The Catholic Church tried to further control the spread of Protestantism by using The Holy Inquisition. This inquisition worked to persecute those found guilty of heresy.

cards.title: Motives for European Expansion
body: Economic Reasons- from the 14th C onwards, land routes to Asia were blocked by the Byzantine Empire forcing the Europeans to look for new sea routes to expand trade with the East, especially for spices.
Cultural and ideological motives- the pretext used by the Europeans to justify their actions of expansion was to introduce Christianity to the pagan natives outside Europe.
The Three G’s- the three Gs stand for: God (the introduction of Christianity), Glory (praise for their countries), and Gold (wealth).

cards.title: Portugal
body: Portugal dominated the expeditions for exploration because they had superior weapons and knowledge of sea travel.

Prince Henry (The Navigator)- sponsored Portuguese ships along the West African coasts in 1420 and discovered The Gold Coast (present day Ghana), he further provided sailors with support and training.
Bartholomew Diaz- reached the southern tip of South Africa known as The Cape of Good Hope in 1488,
Vasco Da Gama- sailed into India through the Cape in 1497-1498 and returned to Portugal with cargos of spices. The profit he made from the cargos encouraged Portuguese traders to sail into India.
The Portuguese destroyed Arab-Turkish ships and defeated the Turkish and Indian fleet in 1509. They set up trade ports in Goa (India) and the Malay Peninsula and monopolized the spice trade.
Despite their trading posts in Asia, they weren’t powerful enough to colonize large areas in Asia.

body: **Diaz (1488).** Bartholomew Diaz rounded the southern tip of Africa, which he called the Cape of Storms. The Portuguese king renamed it the **Cape of Good Hope** because it opened the hope of a sea route to India. His tired crew forced him to turn back.
**Why it mattered.** It proved that the Atlantic and Indian Oceans were connected, which made **Vasco da Gama's** voyage to India (1497–98) possible.
**Memory trick:** "Henry trained, Diaz turned the Cape (1488), da Gama reached India (1498)."

cards.title: Spain
body: Unlike the Portuguese who reached Asia through the Indian Ocean (eastward), the Spanish tried to reach Asia through the Atlantic Ocean (westward).

Christopher Columbus- was an Italian explorer who sought financial help from Queen Isabella of Spain to reach Asia by sailing westwards. Believing he had reached Asia; he discovered the Americas by mistake in 1492.
Amerigo Vespucci- from Florence, Italy, sailed into the Americas and recognized them new undiscovered lands by writing letters about his voyages. The Americas were named after him.

Europeans called the Americas, The New World, b/c they were opportunities for conquest and exploitation, even though these lands had been homes to ancient civilizations such as the Maya, Aztec, and Inca for centuries.

Ferdinand Magellan- was a Portuguese sea Captain who circumnavigated the world by passing through the southern tip of South America and the Pacific in 1519 under the Spanish flag. He was killed in the Philippine islands.
Border conflict arose between Spain and Portugal regarding their colonies in the Americas, which was resolved by The Line of Demarcation in the Treaty of Tordesillas, 1494.

The Line of Demarcation was an imaginary line that divided their spheres of influence. Unexplored territories east of the line were given to Portugal along with Brazil and the routes to Africa while Spain was given the right over the Americas (west) with the exception of Brazil.

cards.title: The Spanish Empire
body: Spanish Conquistadores (conquerors) brought the end of the American civilizations using guns. In Meso-America, Hernan Cortes was able to destroy the Aztec Empire within three years while Francisco Pizarro took control of the Incan Empire in South America and set up the Spanish colonial administration under the reign of Queen Isabella.

The Native Americans were exposed to European diseases such as Small pox, measles and typhus, which they had no resistance to. Many were massacred by the Conquistadores while those who remained were forced to work on the sugar plantations and the mines owned by the Spanish
In order to destroy the Native American culture, Catholic missionaries began to convert them into Christianity and introduced European social structures, languages and government system.

cards.title: European rivals
body: By the end of the 16th C, NEW European rivals began to compete for the Eastern trade.
In the East, the Spanish controlled the Philippine islands in addition to their territories in the Americas.
English fleet landed in the northwestern coasts of India and set up colonies along the eastern coasts of North America and the plantations of the Caribbean in the 17th C

The Dutch (Netherlands) formed the East Indian Company in 1595 and begun to compete with England and France. In the West, The Dutch trade Empire in the Americas declined due to the rivalries with the English and the French. Their colony New Netherland (modern New York) was seized by the English along with Virginia, Massachusetts Bay, the eastern coasts of North America and set up sugar plantations in the Caribbean.
During the 1600s, the French colonized parts of the modern-day Canada and the state of Louisiana (North America).

cards.title: Effects of European Expansion
body: Growth of European Economy- Europe imported agricultural products such as potatoes, maize, tobacco, chocolate and sugar cane, large quantities of gold and silver from the American mines. Gold and silver were used as currency.

Decline of European cities- major trade routes shifted from the Mediterranean region to the Atlantic Ocean, resulting in the decline of the Italian and German city states and the rise of Atlantic trade ports.
Population growth- Western Europe’s population grew with the availability of additional food supply causing Urbanization.
Establishment of American Colonies- 16th C, Europeans established many trade colonies in the Americas. The Colonies were new territories in North America under direct government control.

The development of international trade- the rise of the American trade colonies led to the rise of international trade and commercial Capitalism. The colonies became the sources of raw materials and markets for finished goods.
A Colony is a settlement of people living in the new territory linked to the parent country by trade and direct government control.

lessons.title: Africa During the Era of the Slave Trade

cards.title: The Slave Trade
body: Slavery had been practiced all over the world since the ancient times. In Africa, slaves were the prisoners of war and were sold as domestic workers to Arabia. Europeans sought gold in Africa until they began trading slaves.
16th C, sugar plantations grew in Brazil and the Caribbean and they needed labor but the native laborers had low immunity. This increased the demand for African slaves.
In 1518, the Spanish first shipped African slaves to the Americas and over the next 2 centuries the trade grew into a triangular trade connecting Europe, Africa, and America.

The Triangular Trade- European merchants brought manufactured goods such as guns and clothes to Africa and traded them for cargos of slaves who were sold in the Americas. Then they took raw materials such as tobacco, molasses (used to refine raw sugar), sugar, and raw cotton from the American plantations to Europe for manufacturing.

About 12-15 million African slaves were brought into the Americas between the 16thC-19thC. One of the reasons for the high numbers was high death rate among the slaves due to diseases, hunger and harsh working environment.

During the early years, Europeans bought slaves from the African slave markets in the coasts in return for gold and guns. But as the demand for African slaves increased in the American plantations, they moved inland into African villages in search for slaves.

cards.title: Effects of Slave Trade
body: Depopulation in particular African regions.

cards.title: Political and social structures
body: Europeans didn’t have much direct influence in Africa except for the few places they settled in such as South Africa and Mozambique.

During the 16th C, monarchy was the most common government system in Africa. States like the kingdom of Benin were highly centralized, while the states of Ashanti were collections of small principalities but majority of the Africans lived in small political units like villages let by elders.
Foreign influences- European presence in Africa caused changes such as;
The shift of trade routes from the Sahara to the coasts weakened trans-Saharan trade empires such as the Songhai empire leading to the rise of a new Moroccan dynasty in the 16th C.
Religion was greatly influenced by foreigners; Islam had more impact than Christianity in Northern Africa and later spread west and east.
The Portuguese begun missionary activities in Africa to spread Christianity while the other Europeans were more interested in slave trade and economic exploitations.

cards.title: Completing this point: changes brought by foreign influence in Africa
body: **Change 1 – trade routes moved.** Trade shifted from the Sahara to the coasts, weakening trans-Saharan empires such as **Songhai**, which fell to a Moroccan invasion in 1591.
**Change 2 – religion.** Islam had the greater impact, spreading from North Africa to West and East Africa; Portuguese missionaries spread Christianity on parts of the coast.
**Change 3 – the slave trade.** Most other Europeans were interested in trade and exploitation, above all the **Atlantic slave trade**, which caused wars and population loss.
**Change 4 – new crops.** Maize and cassava were introduced from the Americas.

cards.title: A. The French Wars of Religion (1562-1598)
body: It was fought between the Catholics and the Huguenots (French Protestants) for about 30 years. It only ended when Henry VI issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, which recognized Catholicism as the official religion of France and allowed the Huguenots the right of worship.

cards.title: Causes
body: 1. French kings started persecuting Protestants to stop its spread.
2. The rise of the Huguenots, French Protestants influenced by John Calvin, mostly made up of the nobles who opposed the monarchial rule of the kings.
3. Competition between the Catholics and the Calvinists to acquire followers.

cards.title: B. Dutch-Spanish war (1566-1609)
body: King Philip II (1556-1598), the son of Charles V, brought political and cultural greatness in Spain. To consolidate his inheritance from his father (Spain, the Netherlands, Italy, and the Americas), he insisted on strict Catholicism and strong monarchial authority.

cards.title: Causes
body: 1. Philip II attempted to strengthen his rule by crushing Calvinism in the Netherlands (made up of 17 provinces).

2. Calvinist nobles of the Northern provinces attacked Catholic churches and statues in 1566. Philip sent 10,000 troops to crush the rebellion and fought until 1609. The war ended with a 12-year truce and the United Provinces of the Netherlands was created.

cards.title: C. Spanish-English naval war
body: Elizabeth Tudor (1558- 1603) led a protestant rule in England. She exercised a moderate foreign policy by shifting sides between Spain and France to prevent either of them from being too powerful. But King Philip of Spain had had a long term plan to invade England in order to;
1. Safeguard Spanish merchant ships and colonies in the Americas from British raids.
2. Depose the Protestant rule of Queen Elizabeth I.
3. Restore Catholicism in England
In 1588, Philip tried to invade England with the Spanish Armada (of more than 200 warships) but was defeated by the English navy in the English Channel with more than 100 of the ships destroyed.
The Spanish- English war created the shift of power from Spain to England and France.

cards.title: Completing this point: why Philip II attacked England, and what followed
body: **Philip's three aims.** (1) To protect Spanish treasure ships and colonies in the Americas from English raids (by "sea dogs" such as Francis Drake); (2) to remove the Protestant Queen Elizabeth I; (3) to bring Catholicism back to England.
**The Armada (1588).** More than 200 Spanish warships sailed for England but were defeated in the English Channel by the faster English navy and by storms; more than 100 ships were lost.
**The result.** Spain's power began to decline and leadership passed to **England and France**.
**Memory trick:** "Ships, Queen, Church" – Philip's three reasons.

cards.title: Completing this point: Europe's crisis, 1560–1650
body: **1. Inflation (rising prices).** The flood of gold and silver from the Americas raised prices.
**2. Population pressure, then decline.** Population grew from about 60 million (1500) to 85 million (1600), then fell by 1650 because of war, plague and famine, causing social tension.
**3. The witchcraft trials.** More than 100,000 people were accused of witchcraft and almost 30,000 were executed (burned or hanged) before the trials declined after 1650.

**4. Religious wars.** The **Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)** began as Catholic Habsburgs against Protestant (Calvinist) nobles in Bohemia and drew in Denmark, Sweden, France and Spain. It was the most destructive European war up to then, fought mostly in Germany.
**5. Revolution in England.** The civil war and the revolutions of the 17th century.

cards.title: B. The Witchcraft Trials
body: New religious enthusiasm against the ancient beliefs of witchcraft and magic led to the Inquisition to hunt those who were believed to have practiced witchcraft.

Thousands of people were charged with witchcraft and almost 30,000 of them were executed by either burning of hanging. Those actions brought fear and disturbances in the European societies until the governments lost interest in the trials in around 1650.

cards.title: C. The Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) – Causes
body: The spread of Calvinism all over Europe in the 1600s.

While recognizing Lutheranism in Germany, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) didn’t include Calvinism. The conflict between the Calvinists and the Catholic Church begun in Bohemia (Czech Republic) against the Hapsburg dynasty (Austria) and Holy Roman Empire. The revolution later spread into Denmark, Sweden, France, and Spain.

Most of the war was fought on German soil but the greatest human loss was in the Holy Roman Empire. The war ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia allowing all German states to choose their own religions and it recognized the political independence of the 300 states within the Holy Roman Empire.
This became the end of the Empire and emergence of modern nation-states.

cards.title: D. English Revolutions in the 17th C – Causes
body: Disputes between the King and the Parliament arose after the death of Elizabeth I in 1603. The Stuart dynasty led by King James I of Scotland (Elizabeth’s cousin) rose to power in England. But his idea of divine rights of kings was rejected by the Parliament because they believed the King or Queen and the Parliament should rule together.
Puritans (English Protestants inspired by Calvinists) members of the House of Commons, wanted a separate church from the Catholic Church of England.

The English civil war of 1642 was fought between the Cavaliers or Royalists (the supporters of King Charles I, the son of James I) and the Roundheads (supporters of the Parliament), after Charles rejected of the Parliament’s petition against tax laws, because like his father, Charles believed in the divine rights of the kings.

The Parliament won the war led by Oliver Cromwell and Charles I was executed in 1649. Monarchy was abolished making England a Republic or a commonwealth. But after the death of Cromwell in 1658, the Monarchy was once again restored under the rule of Charles II (son of Charles I).

Charles’s brother James II was a devoted Catholic whose monarchial rule frightened the Parliament when his son was born, thus the English nobles invited Dutch Protestant leaders William and Mary to invade England in 1688. King James escaped to France; this revolution is known as the Glorious Revolution.

In 1689, Mary and William were crowned the Queen and King of England by the Parliament. They passed The Bill of Rights recognizing the Parliament’s rights to make laws and levy taxes. It replaced the divine right of kings by a government system based on the rule of law, a freely elected Parliament, and limited Constitutional Monarchy.

cards.title: The Rise of Absolute Monarchies
body: After the religious wars, the power of the monarchs was increased to achieve stable socio-economic conditions leading to the rise of Absolutism in the 17th C. Absolutism is a government system in which the ruler holds total power and a divine right to rule. Such rulers can make laws, impose taxes, lead the army and determine their own foreign policies

cards.title: France under Louis XIV (1661-1715)
body: Louis XIV rose to power in 1643 but he was only four years old thus power was given to Cardinal Mazarin, the chief minister who was able to crush the nobles who revolted against the monarchy.
Louis took over in 1661 after the death of Mazarin and desired to be the one and only ruler of France. He built a long-standing army of 400,000.
As the leader of the Bourbon dynasty, he tried to dominate European affairs by waging four wars from 1667-1713. He died in 1715 leaving France surrounded by enemies and in a great debt.

cards.title: Absolutism in Central and Eastern Europe – Prussia
body: Out of the 300 German states, the Prussian State emerged under Frederick William The Great Elector in the 17th C. it had the fourth largest army in Europe with 40,000 troops and a civil administration to levy taxes for the army.
The government officials were chosen from the Prussian aristocracy known as the Junkers who served as army officers. Frederick was replaced by his son King Frederick I.

cards.title: Austria
body: As one of the 300 German states, the Hapsburg dynasty of Austria had played a major role in the Holy Roman Empire E.g., Charles V. But after the Thirty Years War, they had lost their German Empire.
They later created the Austrian Empire in Eastern and Southeastern Europe in present day Austria, Czech Republic, and Hungary. They followed a less centralized absolute monarchy.

cards.title: Russia under Peter the Great
body: A new state emerged in the 15th C in Russia led by the Principality of Muscovy and its grand dukes. The first ruler was Ivan IV who was given the title Czar (Caesar) in 1533.

Ivan crushed the power of the Boyars (nobles) and expanded the Russian territories eastwards. The dynasty ended in 1598 putting Russia in a period of Anarchy (the absence of a government) known as the Times of Troubles.

The period of Anarchy ended with the election of Michael Romanov of the Romanov Dynasty as the new czar in 1613. The dynasty lasted until 1917; one famous leader was Peter the Great who rose to power in 1689.

Peter was an absolute monarch like his predecessors who ruled by dividing Russia into provinces. After visiting the west, he westernized Russia and modernized his army and navy, he also built the city of St. Petersburg, which remained as Russian capital until 1918.

lessons.title: The Development of Art and Political Thought

cards.title: A. Artistic Development
body: A new movement known as Mannerism emerged in Italy in the 1520s and 1530s replacing the Renaissance art, it used elongated figures.

In the 16th C, Mannerism was replaced by a new movement known as Baroque which begun in Italy and eventually spread into Europe and Latin America. The Baroque paintings had dramatic effects and rich details while, the architecture reflected the power of the leaders.

cards.title: B. Literature
body: 16th-17th C, a Cultural Flowering took place in England during the Elizabeth Era (1558-1603), where drama grew as the most popular form of literature. The remarkable works of William Shakespeare showed great language skills and knowledge of Human psychology.
Spanish literature also saw its golden age in this era as drama and novel writing flourished. The works of Miguel de Cervantes is an example.

cards.title: C, Political Thoughts
body: The English revolutions of the 17th C brought different ideas from two English thinkers:

Thomas Hobbs wrote Leviathan, a book dealing with political disorder because he was worried about the revolutionary disturbances in England. He believed that before social organization, human life was solitary, poor, nasty and short as humans were guided by a ruthless struggle for self-preservation instead of reason. Thus, absolute rule was needed to preserve order in the society and suppress rebellion.

John Locke wrote the Two Treatises of Government, in which he argued against Hobbs’s idea of the absolute rule of one person. Locke believed that before social organization, humans lived in a state of equality and freedom, but they needed governments to protect their rights based on a mutual obligation with in the state of nature. Locke supported the demands for Constitutional government, the rule of law and the protection of rights.

cards.title: Completing this point: Hobbes versus Locke
body: **Hobbes' conclusion.** In the state of nature life was "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short". **Thus** people made a **social contract**: to stop destroying each other, they agreed to be ruled by an **absolute ruler** with unlimited power, and rebellion had to be suppressed. Absolute power was the price of order.

**Locke's answer.** People are naturally equal and free, with **natural rights to life, liberty and property**. Government is a contract to protect those rights, and if a ruler breaks it, the people may **overthrow** him.
**Why it matters.** Locke's ideas inspired the American Declaration of Independence and the French Revolution.
**Memory trick:** "Hobbes = Hold power (absolutism); Locke = Liberty (rights)."
