cards.title: Rise of the Ottoman Turks
body: A group of Pastural Turks under their leader Osman built their power in the northwest corner of the Anatolian Peninsula. The land was given to them as a reward for helping the Seljuks fight against the Mongols in the 13thC.
The decline of the Seljuks in the 14thC motivated their expansion into the Balkans (southeast Europe) which had been controlled by the Byzantine Empire for centuries.

Ottoman rulers claimed the title of Sultan and began to build a strong military by developing an elite guard called Janissaries (Christian converts serve as soldiers) and mastering new technologies. The Ottomans expanded their rule for over 300 years, to include large areas of Western Asia as well as North Africa and additional lands in Europe.
Under Mehmet II, the Ottoman Empire defeated the Byzantine Empire on May 29, 1453 and seized Constantinople. And made Constantinople (later renamed Istanbul) their capital.

1514-1517, Sultan Selim I took control of Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Arabia. After controlling the holy cities of Islam Jerusalem, Makah (Mecca), and Medina, Selim declared himself as a caliph, defender of the faith and successor to Muhammad. His successors expanded towards the African coasts and the strait of Gibraltar (southern Liberia).

Administration- The Ottomans ruled through local rulers, the central government appointed officials called Pashas, who collected taxes, maintained law and order, and were directly responsible to the sultan’s court in Constantinople.
Suleiman I the Magnificent led the Ottomans attacked Europe and controlled Hungary, Austria in 1520 but were defeated in Vienna and the Mediterranean by the Spanish army twice in 1529 and 1571.

During the first half of the seventeenth century, the expansion of the Ottoman Empire stopped due to internal problems. They tried again in 1683, but were defeated again in Hungary by European forces.

The Sultan was the head of the Ottoman political and military system and in lived the royal palace with his private domain called Harem for his many wives. The grand vizier served as the Sultan’s chief minister and advisor. The empire was divided to districts led by senior official- bureaucrats, trained in the schools for officials in Istanbul, and were given land by the sultan.

Society and Culture- The Ottomans were Sunni Muslims. But were generally tolerant of non-Muslims (as long as they paid tax).The society was divided by occupation into 4 main occupational groups: peasants, artisans, merchants, and pastoral peoples. Women were allowed to own and inherit property and even serve as senior officials and governors.
Economy- starting from the period from Mehmet II the production of pottery; rugs, silk, and other textiles; jewelry; and arms and armor flourished.
Architecture was their greatest contribution, they built magnificent mosques.

cards.title: Decline
body: 1. Weak sultans gave the power to their ministers, who exercised it as they wished.
2. Loss of some territories as the central bureaucracy lost its links with the rural areas
3. Corruption of local officers as the official training schools declined
4. Corruption and constant wars exhausted the imperial treasury.

cards.title: The Rise of Safavid dynasty
body: The fall of the empire of Timur Lenk (Tamerlane), the areas previously under the Mongol Empire fell into anarchy until the coming of the Safavids in the 16thC. The Safavids were Shiite Muslims formed into a dynasty by Shah Ismail who was the descendant of Safi al-Din (leader of Turkish groups in Azerbaijan).

In 1501 Ismail controlled Iran and Iraq and called himself Shah (King). He sent Shiite preachers to Anatolia and tried to convert the Sunnis and massacred those who refused in Baghdad in 1508. This led to war with the Ottoman sultan Selim I, the Ottomans defeated the Safavids in Persia at the battle of Tabriz. But the Safavids regained Tabriz a few years later.
Similar to the Sultan of the Ottomans, the Shah claimed to be the leader of all Muslims.
In 1580s the capital of the Safavids changed from city of Tabriz to city of Isfahan (Iran) due to the attacks of the Ottomans.
Shah Abbas (1588-1629) led the Safavids into the golden age by strengthening his army using latest weapons and training administrators and built the city of Isfahan

Society and Culture- Persia under the Safavids was a mixed society of Turkish and Persian (majority). The upper class was made up of the shah, the middle class was made up of bureaucracy and landed class and the common people were in the lower class. Shia-Islam was the state religion.
Economy- was based on Trade and manufacturing. They had great knowledge of science, medicine, and mathematics.
Architecture- well-planned cities with bazaars, palaces, mosques. Moreover silk weaving and carpet weaving flourished.
Decline (1629) - 1. Weak rulers after shah Abbas
2. Afghan invasion during the reign of Shah Hussein and controlled Isfahan

cards.title: Mogul India (1500)
body: The Indian subcontinent had been divided into Hindu and Muslim kingdoms until the coming of the Mogul dynasty which united India in 1500.

The Moguls came from the mountains north of Indus valley, the dynasty was founded by Babur (son of Timur-Lenk), his mother was descendant of Genghis Khan. He captured Kabul (Afghanistan) in 1504 and entered India 13 years later using his small but militarily superior army. He controlled Delhi and expanded till his death in1530.
Akbar (the grandson of Babur) took the throne at 14 and created the greatest Empire in India after the Mauryan dynasty. He brought about the golden age in India by;
1. Following the policy of religious tolerance to Hindu practices and Jesuit views of Christianity
2. Trade and manufacturing flourished due to a long period of peace and political stability

Society and Culture- the moguls were Muslims leading large group of Hindus in India but they respected the Hindu practices. The Moguls tried to abolish the custom of suttee (burning a widow alive along with her dead husband).

Architecture: the moguls combined the Persian and Indian style to create magnificent buildings such as the Taj Mahal in Agra, which was built by Shah Jahan in memory of his dead wife Mumtaz Mahal in 1653.
Decline-
1. Aurangzeb adopted the policy of religious intolerance; he forced Hindus to convert into Islam, prohibited the construction of Hindu Temples resulting in Hindu revolts against the Mogul empire
2. Persian attacks on Delhi in 1793

3. The arrival of the British in 1650 and their rivalry with the French in India weakened the Mogul authority. In 1757, the British defeated the moguls in the battle of Plessey, Bengal and gained the right to collect taxes and conduct free trade in India. The British gained from trade and weakened the Mogul rule little by little.

cards.title: Completing these points: Babur's conquests and Akbar's golden age
body: **Babur.** After capturing Kabul, Babur entered India with a small army that had **artillery**, took **Delhi** and ruled the plains of North India, continuing his conquests **until his death in 1530**.

**Akbar's golden age – how he achieved it.** (1) **Conquest** – by 1605 he ruled most of India, the greatest empire since the Mauryas. (2) **Religious tolerance** – he respected Hindu practices and even welcomed Jesuit Christian advisers. (3) **Peace and prosperity** – long political stability let trade and manufacturing flourish; textiles, spices, food products and precious stones were exported for gold and silver.
**Memory trick:** "Akbar's three C's: Conquest, Calm (tolerance), Commerce."

cards.title: The Ming Dynasty (1368-1644)
body: The Mongol Dynasty was overthrown by the Ming Dynasty under Ming Hong Wu (1368-1398). His son Yong Le (1398-1424) became the emperor and built the imperial city of Beijing and moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing in 1421.
Yong Le sent several naval voyages to the Indian Ocean and East African coast such as Zheng He, who voyaged across the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Red Sea with a fleet of 200 ships.
But conservative Confucian believers saw the trade activities and enormous profits obtained from those voyages unworthy and stopped them after the death of Yong Le.

cards.title: Contact with the West
body: The first direct contact with Europe was made in 1514 when a Portuguese fleet arrived in the coast of China, while the Ming’s power was at its highest. The Chinese Emperor was believed to be the ‘Son of Heaven’ while other world rulers were simply his “younger brothers”.
The Portuguese were expelled from Guangzhou (Canton) and were limited to Macao after their trade activities angered the Emperor. Direct trade between Europe and China remained limited.

Christian missionaries such as the Jesuits went to China with new western ideas and instruments such as the clock and adapted Chinese Confucian teachings, books, printing, and architecture. This cultural exchange made China famous in the western world.

Achievements- China extended its rule into Mongolia and central Asia and conquered Vietnam under the Ming dynasty. They also strengthened the Great Wall in the north and made peace with the nomadic tribes that were their enemies.
Administration- They had a centralized bureaucracy run by officials chosen through the civil service examination and a nationwide school system.

Economy- They lived off trade, agriculture, and manufacturing. They increased food production by renovating the Grand Canal and introducing new crops. The period of the Ming dynasty marked a new era of prosperity and greatness.

cards.title: Decline
body: Weak rulers and corrupt government in the late 16th C led into peasant unrest due to high taxes.
Decline in crop yields because of harsh weather and peasant revolts.
Population reduction due to the 1630 epidemic.

Chinese rebel forces captured Beijing in 1644 and overthrew the Ming, creating an opportunity for the Manchus (farming and hunting society from Manchuria, northeast of the Great wall) to create the Qing (pure) dynasty in 1644.

cards.title: The Qing Dynasty
body: After capturing Taiwan, the Qing dynasty suppressed the revolts in China and flourished under strong rulers who pacified China and solved its social and economic problems by maintaining Ming’s political system.
They preserved their Manchurian identity by organizing themselves into large landholding nobility and separate military units called Banners. The Bannermen were the fighting force.
The Manchus dealt with ethnic difference by using the policy of power sharing between all Chinese people.

Kangxi (1661-1722) was one of the greatest emperors of China who ruled for 61 years with great intellect and peace. He tolerated the activities of Christian missionaries in China. But after his death, his successors begun to suppress Christians.

Qianlong (1736-1795) was a weak emperor whose corrupt rule and high taxes led to unrest in the rural areas. Many peasants faced economic hardships because of population growth; the Qing’s attempt to crush the peasant revolts in central China weakened the dynasty.

The Qing stopped giving European’s trade privileges and confined all the trade to a small area. The British accepted the trade until the 18th C but begun to demand more trade rights while, Chinese merchants pressured the Qing to allow British goods.
In 1793, the Qing rejected British request for open trade which led into violence.

cards.title: Tokugawa Japan and Korea
body: Tokugawa Japan- Japan was unified by 3 leaders after the collapse of the Kamakura Shogunate 15thC, put Japan in chaos.
Oda Nobunaga- seized the imperial city of Kyoto and consolidated his power by controlling the Shogun (Military General) and holding actual power while the emperor was nominal.
Toyotomi Hideyoshi- succeeded Nobunaga and set up his capital at Osaka. By 1590, he had persuaded most of the Daimyos (ruling families) of the islands to accept his authority.
Tokogawa Ieyasu- powerful daimyo of Edo (Tokyo) took control of Japan in 1603. Their successors restored central authority with their center at Edo until 1868. The Tokugawa brought the “Great Peace”.

cards.title: Europeans in Japan
body: They accepted Portuguese traders in 1543 because they were fascinated by tobacco, clocks, and other European goods. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi used the new firearms to defeat their enemies and unify the islands.

Francis Xavier was the first Jesuit missionary who arrived in 1549 and converted the local daimyos. By the end of 16th C, many Japanese had become Christians until the Jesuits begun destroying Japanese shrines.

In 1587, Hideyoshi issued an edict prohibited Christian activities in his lands, while Ieyasu expelled all missionaries and begun persecuting Japanese Christians. Only Dutch ships were allowed to dock at Nagasaki harbor.

cards.title: Tokugawa Rule
body: Tokugawa Administration-The Tokugawa set up a feudal system that governed Japan for over 300 years uniting about 250 separate territories called Hans ruled by Daimyos. During the Tokugawa, the Samurai class gradually dissolved.

Economy- Trade and industry flourished with the growing cities of Edo, Kyoto, and Osaka. Edo became one of the largest cities in the world by 1750, where banking flourished, and a new merchant class emerged. Most peasants were forced to become tenants or work as hired help because they couldn’t keep up with declining profits and high taxes; this led into a revolt of almost 7000 peasants.

Society- Social classes were rigid with strict distinctions among the 4 classes: Warriors, Peasants, Artisans, and Merchants, with the emperor and his family at the top and a separate group at the bottom of the structure who worked in garbage disposal or the slaughterhouse. Intermarriage was forbidden. The role of women was restricted while Males had the authority over property, marriage and divorce.

Culture- The rise of popular literature appeared in the cities for entertainment while Poetry was a more serious form of literature. Demand for entertainment gave rise to the theater of Kabuki, emphasizing action, music, and drama.
Japanese art during the Tokugawa rule was enriched by ideas from other cultures, pottery designs from Korea, western medicine, astronomy, and languages.

cards.title: Korea- The Hermit Kingdom
body: The Yi dynasty in Korea remained in power since the 14th C with their capital at Hanyang (modern Seoul). The Yi dynasty took the Tokugawa model of social organization and foreign policy by isolating Korea from the outside world earning the name “the Hermit Kingdom”.
In the late 16th C, Japanese forces invaded Korea, although they were defeated, the Yi dynasty was weakened.
In 1630, Manchu army invaded northern Korea and made the Yi dynasty subject to China.
But aside from the invasions of Japan and China, Korea was largely untouched by European merchants and Christian missionaries.

cards.title: The Scientific Revolution
body: In the Middle Ages, many educated Europeans became more interested in the world around them, but their knowledge was based on the ides of ancient philosophers instead of reason and observation. But several changes in the 15th-16th C encouraged the Medieval philosophers abandon their old views and develop new ones, such as

Renaissance humanists began to master Greek and the works of Ptolemy, Archimedes and Plato. They realized that those philosophers didn’t agree with Aristotle but had similar ideas with the Medieval thinkers.
Technical problems and calculations become easier with the invention of new instruments such the telescope and microscope.
The printing press helped spread new ideas quickly followed by the rediscovery of ancient mathematics.

cards.title: A Revolution in Astronomy
body: Medieval Astronomical discoveries completely changed the existing concept of the universe.

Ptolemy was a great Astronomer of the 2ndC whose ideas along with that of Aristotle and the Christian view were later put in the Ptolemic System. This system believes in the Geocentric view of the Universe where the Earth was the center of the Universe and the Sun revolved around it.

In May 1543, Nicholas Copernicus, a mathematician, believed in the Heliocentric view where the Sun was at the center of the Universe and the Earth revolved around it just as the moon revolves around the planets.
Johannes Kepler came up with studies of planetary motion and supported the Heliocentric view.

Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who provided the answers for, what planets are made of? and the motion of the Universe by inventing the Telescope. Using the telescope, Galileo discovered mountains on the moon, moons revolving around Jupiter and sunspots. He also discovered that all planets were composed of material substances instead of pure orbs of light, according to the Ptolemc system.

The Copernican ideas were rejected by the Catholic church as they shook the Christian ideas. Galileo was arrested by the church and was forced to retrack his ideas. Giordano Bruno was another Italian philosopher who was burned on the stake by the church for his beliefs of infinite universe.
Isaac Newton was a philosopher and a mathematician, who wrote the 3 laws of motion and the force of gravity.

cards.title: Developments in Medicine and Chemistry, 16thC
body: Andreas Vesalius who wrote ‘On the Fabric of the Human Body’ written in 1543, he came up with human anatomy based on conducting accurate examinations on the individual Human organs. But like the past mistakes he believed in the two kinds of blood flowing in the veins and arteries.
William Harvey wrote ‘On the Motion of the Heart and Blood’ in 1628, proved that the same blood flowed I the veins and the arteries.

Robert Boyle was one of the first scientists to conduct controlled experiments on the properties of gases leading to Boyle’s Law. He believed that the volume of gases varies with the pressure exerted on them.
Antoine Lavoisier invented a system of naming the chemical elements, much of which is still used today. He is regarded by many as the founder of modern chemistry.

cards.title: Philosophies
body: Rene Descartes was a French modern rationalist who emphasized on doubt and uncertainty. He talked of the importance of the mind and that he would only accept as true only those things that he can reason out. Descartes has been called the father of modern rationalism. According to Descartes reason is the chief source of knowledge.

“I think therefore I am” is one of the most famous philosophical quotes influenced by Western Philosophy. The quote was used by Descartes to answer the question what warrants the declaration of existence?

cards.title: Women in the Scientific Revolution
body: Margaret Cavendish was a British scientist who wrote a book about experimental philosophy. In Germany 14% of the astronomers were women.

cards.title: The Scientific Method
body: Francis Bacon was a British scientist who believed in experiment and reasoning to learn about nature by conducting systemic observations and carefully organized experiments to test hypotheses to come up with correct principles. Bacon wanted to employ science in industry, agriculture and trade.

New instruments such as the telescope and microscope made observation and calculation easier.
The printing press spread new ideas quickly, together with rediscovered ancient mathematics.

cards.title: the Enlightenment
body: The Enlightenment was an 18thC intellectual movement of philosophers who were greatly impressed with the achievements of the Scientific Revolution. One of the favorite words of these intellectuals was reason, which meant the application of the scientific method to an understanding of all life.
The Enlightenment was especially influenced by the ideas of two 17thC Englishmen, Isaac Newton and John Locke.

Isaac Newton was an English Scientist who saw the physical world and everything in it as a giant machine (the Newtonian world-machine). The intellectuals of the Enlightenment thought they could discover the natural laws that governed human society.
Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) was a French scientist, one of the most influential writers of the French Renaissance he introduced ‘essay’ as new literary genre and the founder of modern skepticism.

John Locke suggested that people were molded by the experiences that came through their senses from the surrounding world. If environments were changed and people were exposed to the right influences, then people could be changed, and a new society would be created.

cards.title: Enlightenment Thinkers and Their Ideas
body: Most of the thinkers of the Enlightenment were French, but some English philosophers.

Montesquieu-his full name was Charles-Louis de Secondat, the Baron de Montesquieu, came from the French nobility. His most famous work ‘The Spirit of the Laws’ was published in 1748. In this study of governments, Montesquieu identified three branches the executive, the legislative (parliament) and judiciary (the court of law).

Voltaire- his real name was François-Marie Arouet, known simply as Voltaire by his pen name. Voltaire was especially well known for his criticism of Christianity and his strong belief in religious tolerance. He strongly advocated against religious intolerance in France.
Denis Diderot is the writer of the Encyclopedia, or Classified Dictionary. Published between 1751 and 1772, the Encyclopedia attacked religious superstition and supported religious toleration.

David Hume (1711–1776), was a Scottish philosopher, historian, economist, and writer known especially for his philosophical empiricism and skepticism. He was one of the most important figures in the history of Enlightenment. ‘A Treatise of Human Nature’ and ‘Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion’ are some of his influential works.

Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher who founded the modern social science of economics. He believed that if individuals were free to pursue their own economic self-interest, all society would eventually benefit thus, the state should not interfere in the economy. This doctrine became known as laissez-faire, a French term meaning to let people do what they want.

cards.title: The Later Enlightenment (1760s)
body: Jean-Jacques Rousseau presented his concept of the Social Contract, published in 1762. Through a social contract, an entire society agrees to be governed by its general will. Individuals who wish instead to follow their own self-interest must be forced to abide by the general will. Thus, liberty is achieved by being forced to follow what is best for “the general will,” because the general will represents what is best for the entire community.

For centuries, male thinkers had argued that the nature of women made them inferior to men and made male domination of women necessary. By the eighteenth century, however, female thinkers began to express their ideas about improving the condition of women.

Mary Wollstonecraft was an English writer who wrote ‘In A Vindication of the Rights of Women’, she argued that the domination of men over women was wrong and that the Enlightenment was based on an ideal of reason in all human beings. Because women have reason, then they are entitled to the same rights as men. She advocated for women’s equal rights in education, as well as in economic and political life.

cards.title: The Social World of the Enlightenment
body: The Enlightenment was not a movement belonging exclusively to the nobles and aristocrats. For example, enlightenment thinkers such as Diderot and Rousseau came from the lower middle class. The movement, however, greatly influenced the aristocrats and upper classes in the larger cities. The common people, especially the peasants, were mostly unaware and little affected by the Enlightenment.

The Salon- Salons were the elegant drawing rooms of the wealthy upper class. Invited guests gathered in these salons and took part in conversations that discussed the new ideas of the philosophe and helped the spread of Enlightenment ideas. Hosts of the salons were mostly wealthy upper-class women.

steps.text: Montesquieu, a French noble, published *The Spirit of the Laws* in 1748.
Studying governments, he identified three branches: the executive, the legislative and the judicial.
Each branch should limit and check the others.
This protects liberty by preventing any one person or group from holding all power.

cards.title: B. War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748)
body: The war started when Maria Theresa succeeded Charles VI as the queen of Austria. King Frederick II of Prussia took the advantage of the succession to invade Austria and he seized Silesia. France joined the war on the side of Prussia, while Britain entered the war on the side of Austria.

The war was fought in Europe, the Far East and North America and only ended with the treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle in 1748. Since all parties were exhausted after seven years of warfare, they agreed to the treaty.

cards.title: C, The Seven Years War (1756-1763)
body: After Prussia refused to hand over Silesia, Maria won a revolutionary diplomacy with France by separating it from Prussia in 1756 and built an army. Thus, the old rivalry replaced by the French-British rivalry over colonial empires and Austria-Prussia over Silesia.

The war started when the alliance of France, Austria and Russia saw Prussia as threat, the British on the other hand allied with Prussia. The war had three major areas of conflict Europe, North America and India in 1756-1763.
The war ended 1763 and all occupied territories were returned to their original owners, the effects include;
France left India to the British by the treaty of Paris
Austria recognized permanent control of Silesia by Prussia
France gave Canada and Mississippi to England.
French gave French Louisiana to Spain.
Spain gave Spanish Florida to England.
By 1763 British become the strongest power in the world.

cards.title: Completing this point: results of the Seven Years' War (1756–1763)
body: **Treaty of Paris (1763) and Hubertusburg.** (1) **France** lost India to Britain; (2) France gave **Canada** and the land east of the Mississippi to Britain; (3) France gave **Louisiana** to Spain; (4) Spain gave **Florida** to Britain; (5) **Austria** accepted Prussia's permanent control of **Silesia**.
**The big result.** Britain became the strongest colonial and naval power in the world.
**A hidden effect.** The war left Britain heavily in debt; its new taxes on the American colonies led to the American Revolution.

cards.title: Motives of Italian Colonialism
body: Imperialism as a mark of prestige- Italy was concerned with achieving the status of the superpowers in Europe
National Unity of Italy- Colonial expansion would direct the people into a common cause and national unity
Demographic motive- between 1861-1911, Italian population showed a significant increase from 25 to 35 million causing shortage of land for settlement.
The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869- increased the strategic importance of Red Sea and Eritrea after the British and French occupied Aden and Egypt respectively
Before the advent of Italy, Eritrea was contested upon by the Abyssinians (Ethiopia), Mahdists (Sudan) and Egypt.

cards.title: Italian Expansion
body: December 15, 1869, Rubbatino Shipping company’s agent, Giuseppe Sapeto bought a land in Assab from local Afar chiefs, Sultan Hassan, and Ibrahim and sold it to the Italian government in March 1882 but faced local opposition from the Afar.

Mahdists were Islamic anti-Egyptian liberation movement in Sudan created in 1882, to remove Egyptian forces from Sudan and Eritrea. Britain also helped Italy in Eritrea to stop French expansion into Eritrea from Djibouti.
February 5, 1885, Admiral Caimi established Italian colonization in Eritrea after Egyptian evacuation, they easily expanded into Ailet, Wia and Sahatit because:
The Great Famine (1888-1892) weakened the ability of Eritreans to resist expansion.
Italians dealt strongly with native resistance.
Eritreans accepted Italian protection from Tigrayan and Egyptian raids.

Emperor Yohannes IV confronted Italian expansion to preserve his feudal interests in Eritrea and sent Ras Alula (of Mereb Millash) to fight the battle of Dogali in 1887. Alula defeated Italian garrisons at Sahatit and limited them to Massawa.
Treaty of Wuchale was signed between the Italians and Menelik II of Shewa (Yohannes’s power rival) in May 1889 facilitating Italian expansion into Eritrea after Yohannes died fighting the Mahdists.

Menelik recognized Italian rule in Eritrea, while Italy recognized Menelik as the Emperor of Abyssinia. Thus, in January 1890 King Umberto declared Eritrea as an Italian colony, the name Eritrea was derived from the name of the sea, Mare Erytrium.
Italy used 3 mechanisms to establish colonies in Eritrea: Purchase of land, military force, and forging alliances with local chiefs.

Article 17 in the Treaty of Wuchale had language complications to trick Menelik. The Italian version stated that” Menelik had to ask Italian permission in any of his foreign affairs”, while the Amharic version stated that “Menelik had the right to seek Italian help if he chooses to”. Menelik found out and this led into the Battle of Adwa (March 1, 1896), where he won and declared The Treaty of Addis Ababa stating:
1, The Mereb-Belesa-Muna line as the border between Italian-Eritrea and Ethiopia
2, Set up other Eritrean borders based on agreements with the British in Sudan and the French in Djibouti

cards.title: Completing these points: why Italy expanded easily, and how Wuchale led to Adwa
body: **Why Italy expanded easily into Ailet, Wia and Sahatit (after 5 February 1885).** (1) The **great famine of 1888–1892** weakened Eritreans' ability to resist; (2) the Italians crushed local resistance harshly; (3) some Eritreans accepted Italian protection against raids from Tigray and from Egypt.

**Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale (May 1889).** The Italian text said Menelik **must** conduct his foreign affairs through Italy (a protectorate); the Amharic text said he **could** use Italy if he wished. When Menelik discovered this, he rejected the treaty.
**What it led to.** The dispute, together with both sides' expansionist ambitions, led to the **Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896)**, where Italy suffered a crushing defeat.

**The Treaty of Addis Ababa (26 October 1896).** Ethiopia recognized Italian Eritrea and the **Mereb–Belesa–Muna line** as the border; other borders were fixed by agreements with Britain (Sudan) and France (Djibouti).
**Memory trick:** "Must or May? – one word, one war (Adwa 1896)."

cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain the motives of Italian colonialism in Eritrea.

steps.text: Prestige: Italy wanted the status of the European great powers.

Population: Italy's population rose from 25 to 35 million (1861–1911), causing land shortage, so settlers needed land.

cards.title: Phases of Italian Colonization
body: 1.The first Phase (1890-1896)- Land Alienation policy focused on creating Italian settlements in Eritrea by confiscating 400,000 hectares in 2 years, this caused shortage of land and poverty. This policy ended quickly due to local opposition.

2.The Second Phase, (1896-early 1930s)- served Italian strategic and economic motives, Eritrea became the source of colonial army (Askaries), where thousands were conscripted and sent into Somalia and Libya or used to ensure stability in the colonies. Italian economic expansion in East Africa was promoted by initiating Infrastructural and industrial developments in Eritrea.

3. The Third Phase, (mid 1930s-1941)- Infrastructural, economic, and military developments grew significantly. Between 1934-1939, the number of Italian settlers in Eritrea grew from 4,600 to 75,000, who mostly lived in the towns and cities.

cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the three phases of Italian colonial policy in Eritrea.

steps.text: First phase (1890–1896): land alienation – about 400,000 hectares confiscated for Italian settlers; ended by local opposition.
Second phase (1896–early 1930s): strategic and economic aims – thousands of Eritreans conscripted as askaris for Somalia and Libya; infrastructure and industry begun.
Third phase (mid-1930s–1941): large infrastructural, economic and military growth.
Italian settlers rose from 4,600 to 75,000 between 1934 and 1939, mostly in towns.

cards.answer: Land alienation (1890–96), askari recruitment and economic development (1896–1930s), then rapid military and economic build-up with mass settlement (1930s–1941).

cards.title: Eritrean Resistance to Italian Rule
body: Causes for Opposition to Italian Rule
There was no major opposition against Italians in Eritrea as many notables allied with them to get protection from Amhara and Mahdists, it begun only after 1890 because of 2 reasons:
Italian attacks and imprisonment of many local chiefs to avoid any resistance, they killed and imprisoned hundreds of chiefs in the island prison of Nakura and Assab.
Italian policy of land alienation and confiscation of huge lands from the natives.

In the highlands, Degiat Kafil Gofar was arrested in Assab for fighting against Italian rule in Keren. Kentibay Hamid Wed Hassan and Mahmud (of Sahil) were sent to Nakura for refusing to pay tribute to the Italians.
Zemat Wedi Ekud and Mohammad Agora (of Barka) opposed Italian activities in Barka and Agordat. Bulgya and Dember Aga from the Nara also showed resistance.
Degiat Abera was another collaborator of Italy who was arrested in 1891 for killing an Italian officer. He allied with Menelik and fought against the Italians from Ethiopia.
Abubakar Ahmed led a Saho revolt and defeated an Italian army. He later died in Battle.

Mohammad Nuri (breaker of Nakura) was a Saho who attacked Italians from Tigray after escaping with 107 prisoners from Nakura. He activities in Senafe and Adi Rosso led the Italians believe that he planned to kill Eritrean governor Fernandino Martini.

Degiat Bahta Hagos - accepted Italian protection and was appointed as the governor (Degiat) of Segeneyti in 1889. But he opposed the 1894 policy of land alienation as portrayed in the message he sent his brother Sengal: “My brother Sengal don’t be too foolish, if a white snake bites, there is no medicine for its venom”. He led a prominent highland revolt but was defeated and killed.

cards.title: Completing this point: Bahta Hagos and the Halay revolt (1894)
body: **Who he was.** Degiat **Bahta Hagos** first welcomed the Italians and was made governor of **Segeneyti** in 1889.

**Why he turned.** In 1893 Italy decided to take one-fifth of the highland farmland, then doubled the area seized – almost all the highland's arable land. Bahta warned his brother: "My brother Sengal, do not be too foolish… if a white snake bites, you cannot find medicine for its venom."

**The revolt.** In **December 1894** he declared revolt against "the white snake", imprisoned the Italian officer Sanguinetti and called the highlands to rise: "I will liberate you from the one who came from overseas to take our rights, seize our lands…".

**Halay.** On **18 December 1894** he attacked the Italian force at **Halay** and caused heavy damage, but Italian reinforcements from Asmara and Massawa arrived, and Bahta was wounded and died. It was a peasant revolt against land alienation, one of the notable anti-colonial revolts of north-east Africa.
**Memory trick:** "White snake = land alienation; Halay = 1894."

cards.title: Model answer: why Eritreans resisted Italian rule after 1890
cards.problem: (Exam question) Why did Eritrean resistance to Italian rule begin after 1890? Give examples of resisters.

steps.text: Before 1890 many notables allied with Italy for protection from Amhara and Mahdist raids.
Reason 1: Italians attacked and imprisoned local chiefs – hundreds were killed or held in the island prisons of Nakura and Assab.
Reason 2: the land alienation policy confiscated huge areas of land.

Examples: Degiat Bahta Hagos (rebelled in 1894 against land alienation), Kentibay Hamid Wed Hassan, Zemat Wedi Ekud, Abubakar Ahmed (Saho revolt) and Mohammad Nuri, who escaped from Nakura with 107 prisoners.

cards.answer: Repression of chiefs and land confiscation turned allies into resisters such as Bahta Hagos, Abubakar Ahmed and Mohammad Nuri.

cards.title: Administration
body: New administrative structures such as Districts led by local chiefs Mislene appointed by Italian administrators (Commissaris), were introduced to keep the local rulers loyal with the Colonial Governor was at the top of the hierarchy. Administrative divisions (Comiissariati) were Hamasien, Seraye, Akkele Guzai, Massawa, Assab, Barka and Keren, Gash and Setit.
The towns were administered by municipalities. With 7 principal towns: Asmara, Massawa, Keren, Dekemhare, Adi Ugri, Adi keih and Assab. Some of the administration codes were:
Italian penal code (for all residents)
Italian civil code (for Italian citizens only)
Sharia and Eritrean customary law for native civil cases

cards.title: Completing these points: the Italian administrative divisions and legal codes
body: **The commissariati changed over time.** Before 1900 there were three centres (Assab, Keren, Asmara). In **1903** there were **seven**: Hamasien, Serae, Akkele Guzai, Massawa, Assab, Barka and Keren. In **1908** Gash and Setit were added (eight), and in **1931** they were reduced to five. Each was led by an Italian **commissario**; districts were under a **residente**, and the **Governor** in Asmara was at the top.
**Towns.** Seven principal towns had municipalities: Asmara, Massawa, Keren, Dekemhare, Adi Ugri, Adi Keih and Assab.

**Legal codes.** The Italian penal code applied to all residents; the Italian civil code only to Italian citizens; **Sharia and Eritrean customary law** for natives' civil cases – one law for colonizers, another for the colonized.

cards.title: Army and Police Forces
body: Askaris and Bandas (irregulars) were recruited from the colonies to fight in Libya and Somalia, 60,000 Eritreans were conscripted during the Italian invasion of Ethiopia in 1935.
The Carabinieri were traditional royal police, while the Polizia Africana Italiana was later setup by Mussolini.

cards.title: Education
body: Traditional education provided by churches and mosques was dominant until 1909, where separate schools and curriculums were introduced for Italian and Eritrean students.
There were four government schools with education limited up to the fourth grade because the need for native education was to train limited number of loyal servants.

cards.title: Racial Laws
body: Racial attitudes had always been part of the Italian colonial rule, but they were formalized through the Fascist Racial laws of 1935, to separate colonizers and the colonized by prohibiting interracial marriages and reserving public places for Italians by restricting native entry.
Economy- Italians invested in Eritrean economy because their objectives in Eritrea were:
Land Alienation for Italian settlement
Source of raw materials and market for finished Italian products
Use Eritrea as a springboard for colonial expansion in Ethiopia

cards.title: Completing this point: Italy's economic aims in Eritrea
body: **Aim 1 – land for settlers.** Land alienation to settle Italian farmers.
**Aim 2 – raw materials and markets.** Eritrea would supply raw materials and buy Italian manufactured goods.

**Aim 3 – a springboard.** Eritrea would be a base for conquering Ethiopia, which explains the big investment in roads, the Massawa–Asmara railway and the cableway in the 1930s before the 1935 invasion.
**Memory trick:** "Land, Trade, Launchpad."

cards.title: Transport and Communication
body: Between 1890-1941 a total of 710 km roads was constructed along with 1353 km seasonal roads, connected by bridges and tunnels along with a 71 km Asmara-Massawa cableway (teleferika), 248 km long Massawa-Aqordat railroad.
About 600 miles long Asmara-Addis Ababa telegraph lines, 25 post offices, and 17 telephone stations along with regular air transport (1935) were introduced in Eritrea.

cards.title: Ports
body: Massawa and its port served as the Italian capital until its destruction due to the 1921 earthquake. It was restored and a modern port was built with a budget of 35.5 million lire.
Since Assab wasn’t as important, minimal projects were carried out including the Assab-Dessie road and a few salt and iron mining bays.

cards.title: Agriculture
body: Agriculture declined as cash crop production replaced food crops under the Italian policy. Agriculture also declined as 40.3% of the work force were conscripted in the colonial army.
But Italian colonization modernized commercial farming and domestic animal’s vaccination as exemplified in the Coffee, Sisal and Cotton plantations all over Eritrea.

cards.title: Trade and industry
body: Italians begun to exploit minerals and other products after taking over trade in the port of Massawa from Arabs and some locals, but trade showed a rapid development after 1935.

Eritrea only served as a source of raw material during the first and second phases, but from 1930 onwards industrialization became vital to meet the demands of Italians soldiers to undergo Italian invasion of Ethiopia. Eritrean industrial firms grew from 56 to 2,198.

cards.title: Urbanization
body: Most of the construction of Asmara was finished by 1930s with separate residential areas for the whites and the natives, this increased population and gave way to further investments in Keren, Assab, Mendefera, and Aqordat.
Military installations, airports and businesses expanded as Eritrea became Italian economic center for Ethiopian exploitation.
